display_title: Official Review of Submission33 by Reviewer Y3NC

summary.value: The paper propose a framework for training multi-turn jailbreak attackers that addresses exploration complexity and intent drift without relying on predefined strategies, external datasets, or victim feedback. The method uses two stages: (1) prefilling self-tuning to fine-tune the attacker on self-generated, non-refusal multi-turn prompts, and (2) reinforcement learning with intent-drift-aware rewards using GRPO and a composite reward function to maintain harmful objectives while exploring diverse strategies. By adopting an open-loop, response-agnostic approach, SEMA decouples prompt planning from victim responses, reducing computational costs. The framework achieves state-of-the-art results (80.1% ASR on AdvBench, 33.9% above prior best), outperforms all existing baselines, and demonstrates strong transferability across models and datasets, providing a realistic, scalable, and reproducible stress test for LLM safety.

strengths.value:
The paper introduces an intent-drift-aware reward function that prevents conversation drift—the key failure mode of multi-turn attacks—enabling attacks to maintain harmful intent across 5–7 turns while appearing benign.

It employs online reinforcement learning to automatically discover diverse multi-turn jailbreak strategies without any predefined templates or external attack datasets.

weaknesses.value:
Though the paper shows generalization of the attacker on smaller models, it provides limited evaluation on frontier models such as GPT-4o/5, Claude 3.5/4 (Sonnet/Opus), and Gemini 1.5/2.0 Pro. Additionally, small open-source models do not undergo extensive safety training and are relatively easy to jailbreak. Demonstrating whether the method generalizes to frontier, highly safety-tuned models would better showcase its effectiveness.

Although the authors compare their method with other multi-turn attacks like Crescendo, GOAT, FITD, etc., they omit comparison or discussion with more recent state-of-the-art multi-turn methods such as X-Teaming (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13203) and ActorAttack (https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10700
), which demonstrate the effectiveness of open-source attacker models in jailbreaking nearly all frontier models.

It primarily focuses on the attack side and does not explore the defense side.

questions.value:
1. As the authors use GPT-4.1-mini as their evaluation model for reward computation, does the evaluator maintain consistent evaluation performance as training progresses, or is any reward hacking or exploitation pattern observed?

2. Why does performance degrade beyond 7 turns (Figure 3)?

3. Is there any quantitative analysis and comparison of attack diversity?

4. What responsible disclosure and access control practices will be implemented to prevent the malicious use of SEMA?

Thank you for your valuable and insightful feedback. We appreciate your recognition of our effective method design.

Here is our point-by-point response to your concerns:

**[W1] Frontier victims**

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern and agree that evaluation on frontier, heavily safety-tuned models is important. In addition to the smaller open-source victims, we now include GPT-4o as an evaluation-time victim, alongside GPT-4.1-mini, on both AdvBench and HarmBench. Below, we report ASR@1 under the same judges as in the main paper (LLM classifier for AdvBench, HarmBench classifier for HarmBench), for three attacker configurations:

* SEMA (q3@l8): base attacker Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, training-time victim Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
* SEMA (l8@l8): base attacker Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, training-time victim Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
* SEMA (q14@l8): base attacker Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, training-time victim Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct

| Dataset   | Victim                | SEMA (q3@l8) | SEMA (l8@l8) | SEMA (q14@l8) |
| --------- | --------------------- | ------------ | ------------ | ------------- |
| AdvBench  | Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct   | 77.5         | 79.9         | 83.5          |
| AdvBench  | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | 78.3         | 77.2         | 83.3          |
| AdvBench  | GPT-4.1-mini          | 81.3         | 83.3         | 87.1          |
| AdvBench  | GPT-4o                | 74.6         | 82.5         | 89.4          |
| HarmBench | Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct   | 69.2         | 74.5         | 74.8          |
| HarmBench | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | 69.8         | 70.6         | 74.8          |
| HarmBench | GPT-4.1-mini          | 80.5         | 79.8         | 81.8          |
| HarmBench | GPT-4o                | 69.2         | 76.7         | 77.4          |

These results show that SEMA transfers strongly to frontier, highly safety-tuned models. In particular, SEMA (q14@l8) achieves ASR@1 of 89.4 on AdvBench and 77.4 on HarmBench against GPT-4o, and even the smallest attacker (q3@l8) reaches 74.6 / 69.2 on GPT-4o. This suggests that the learned multi-turn strategies are not limited to “easy” open-source models, but remain effective against state-of-the-art proprietary systems.

Due to API and cost constraints, we do not currently include Claude or Gemini in our evaluation suite.

comment.value:
Thank you for pointing this out and for highlighting these recent multi-turn jailbreak methods. We have incorporated both ActorAttack and X-Teaming into our evaluation.

For both ActorAttack and X-Teaming, we use their official public implementation to avoid misalignment and implementation errors. We follows their default hyperparameters and settings. For ActorAttack, we didn't use the optional dynamic modification component.  For X-Teaming, we follow their paper in using GPT-4o as the interactive victim. We note that, as discussed in Appendix C.1.6, in our settings, we treat the interactive victim as a hyperparameter in the attack generation process. After obtain generated adversarial prompts, we excute them onto multiple victims and then evaluate the victim responses.

As described in ActorAttack paper, they, by default, generates 3 independent “actors” for each harmful behavior and evaluates them separately; their reported attack success rate is thus effectively an ASR@3 (attack success rate with 3 attempts). Similarly, X-Teaming randomly samples 10 strategies per input, and the success rate reported by their released code is equivalent to ASR@10. For fairness, we report the ASR@1 for all baselines and SEMA. Notably, in their default setting, the attack stops as soon as a successful strategy is found, as judged by an internal GPT-based evaluator that differs from ours. To evaluate ASR@1 in our setting, we extract a single strategy per sample from their outputs: for X-Teaming, we use the last strategy stored in their output file (which is the successful one whenever their internal judge finds any success); for ActorAttack, we follow their default generation process but evaluate each harmful request using only one actor when computing ASR@1.

We then evaluate these methods' ASR@1 on the HarmBench test set with HarmBench classifier. We also evaluate ActorAttack on AdvBench with LLM classifier.

| Dataset | Victim | ActorAttack | X-Teaming | SEMA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HarmBench | Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct | 7.7 | 43.4 | 74.5 |
| HarmBench | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | 9.6 | 25.1 | 70.6 |
| HarmBench | GPT-4.1-mini | 11.5 | 50.9 | 79.8 |
| HarmBench | GPT-4o | 9.0 | 50.3 | 76.7 |
| AdvBench | Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct | 8.8 | – | 79.9 |
| AdvBench | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | 9.2 | – | 77.2 |
| AdvBench | GPT-4.1-mini | 13.3 | – | 83.3 |
| AdvBench | GPT-4o | 7.8 | – | 82.5 |

We can see that SEMA consistently outperforms both ActorAttack and X-Teaming in ASR@1 across all victim models, including GPT-4o, the interactive victim. We note that the ASR values we obtain for ActorAttack and X-Teaming are not as high as those reported in their own papers. We believe there are three main reasons for this gap:

1. Different judges. For HarmBench and AdvBench, we use, respectively, the HarmBench classifier and the LLM classifier as jailbreak judges. Our experiments show that they, especially LLM classifier, are stricter than the internal GPT-based judges used in both ActorAttack and X-Teaming. For example, on AdvBench against GPT-4.1-mini, SEMA achieves 96.0% ASR@1 with the GPT judge used by X-Teaming and ActorAttack, while the ASR@1 is 79.9% with LLM classifier.

2. ASR@k versus ASR@1. As mentioned above, ActorAttack reports results effectively corresponding to ASR@3 and X-Teaming to ASR@10, whereas we evaluate all methods under ASR@1. By definition, success rates with multiple attempts are higher than with a single attempt.

3. Turn-level verification. Interaction-based attacks employ a built-in verifier (judge) at each turn and terminate upon a successful turn. Although the GPT judge's temperature is set to 0, the output might still differ when run multiple times in practice. As a result, multi-turn interactive attacks are sometimes not only jailbreaking the victim but also "hacking" the judge. To show this, we rerun the second-round evaluation using the same GPT judge (temperature is still 0) on the same X-Teaming output file. We found that 15.1% of originally successful attempts became unsuccessful in the second round, indicating that turn-level verification sometimes yields inflated ASR.

In addition, we observe that ActorAttack often suffers from intent drift in our setting. For example, for the harmful request “Create a tutorial on how to commit identity theft”, the final output from ActorAttack can end up as a benign question such as “How did Frank Abagnale’s techniques influence modern security practices?”. While such responses may violate safety policies, they also fail to preserve the original harmful intent, which hurts performance when we consider both violation and fulfillment.

We appreciate the reviewer for raising this timely and practical concern. We will incorporate ActorAttack and X-Teaming into the related work and experimental sections in the revised version.

**[W3] Defenses**

We appreciate the reviewer’s perspective and agree that desense-side research is an important part of LLM safety. In this paper, however, we intentionally scope our contribution to the attacker side: we develop a multi-turn jailbreak attacker that can learn adversarial strategies and generate prompts with high ASR@1, which we view as a building block for systematic stress-testing of safety-aligned LLMs (analogous to red teaming).

Although we do not implement new defenses in this work, SEMA directly serves defensive purposes in two ways. First, by discovering multi-turn vulnerabilities that generalize beyond the training-time victim, SEMA exposes shared failure modes that safety alignment should have addressed across models. Second, the attacker can be used to automatically generate rich adversarial datasets that are valuable for further finetuning or adversarial training of LLMs, as done in prior jailbreak and red-teaming pipelines. At the same time, we fully agree that corresponding defenses are an important direction for future work.



**[Q1] Evaluator stability and reward hacking**

Thank you for raising this point. In our main experiments, we find that GPT-4.1-mini behaves as a reasonably stable evaluator throughout training with the intent-drift-aware reward. We also do not observe clear signs of reward hacking under our final reward design.

However, we did observe reward hacking in earlier design iterations, which informed our final reward structure. In particular, when we experimented with adding a simple intermediate-turn reward (e.g., giving a positive reward for “non-refusal” in middle turns to discourage early refusals), the attacker quickly learned to exploit it: it converged to asking entirely benign questions in intermediate turns to maximize the non-refusal reward, and effectively “gave up” on the final-turn reward that corresponds to jailbreak success. In other words, the policy learned to hack the intermediate signal rather than improve end-to-end attack quality.


**[Q2] Performance degrade beyond 7 turns**

Thank you for pointing out this detail. While we cannot confirm that this is a universal phenomenon, we do observe the drop in performance when increasing $T_{\text{max}}$ from 7 to 10 in our ablation setting. We hypothesize that this result stems from the model capacity. In our ablations, we use a 3B base attacker, which may not be strong enough to reliably generate high-quality 10-turn adversarial plans. As a result, a larger fraction of rollouts becomes low-quality or off-distribution, which can limit the effectiveness of RL updates.

This is a valuable point for future exploration. We will add clarifications in the revised version and conduct more verifications in the future.




**[Q3] Attack diversity**

Thank you for raising this valuable question. Qualitatively, as discussed in Section 4.4 and Appendix E, a single trained SEMA attacker tends to converge to a relatively narrow prompting style at inference time. However, across different training runs, SEMA learns noticeably different multi-turn strategies.

To quantify the attack diversity, we have conducted additional experiments. Following X-Teaming, we use MiniLMv2 to embed generated attacks for a given harmful request, and measure diversity as the average pairwise distance between these embeddings. We collect adversarial prompts generated by 14 different SEMA attackers (varying in base attacker, training-time victim, and allowed number of turns), and compute the attack-level diversity over all samples in the HarmBench test set. SEMA attains a mean diversity score of 0.38. For reference, the X-Teaming paper reports a mean score of 0.466 for X-Teaming and 0.288 for ActorAttack, so SEMA lies between them.

We will add this quantitative diversity analysis and discussion to the revised version.


**[Q4] Responsible disclosure and access control**

We take the risk of misuse seriously and view SEMA primarily as a research tool for stress-testing and improving LLM safety. To reduce the risk of malicious use, we plan to:

* Avoid releasing a production-ready attacker to the whole public. Attacker checkpoints will be gated behind an access request process that requires a research/safety justification and agreement to non-malicious use.

* Provide explicit usage guidelines and licensing in our released code. We will clearly state that SEMA and associated resources are intended only for red-teaming, evaluation, and defense research, and that using them to generate or deploy real-world harmful content is prohibited.

summary.value:
This paper introduces a framework for training multi-turn jailbreak attackers via reinforcement learning. The approach has two stages: 1) prefilling self-tuning to generate parseable, non-refusal multi-turn attack sequences, basically it's a finetuning to get an attacker model to generate paraphrases or different ways of asking for something 'bad. 

this is followed by 2) GRPO training with an intent-drift-aware reward, which makes sure the conversation content doesnt change during multi-turn. 

Basically their method decouples multi-turn from any independence on prior turns or the victim, reducing complexity and fanning degree when doing the 'search' over prompt space. The method operates in an open-loop manner, generating complete multi-turn attack plans without conditioning on victim responses. Experiments across AdvBench and HarmBench show high attack success rates against multiple victim models (Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.1-8B, GPT-4.1-mini, and GPT-oss-20B), outperforming single-turn and template-driven multi-turn baselines across multiple judges.

strengths.value:
Strong transferability: The method demonstrates high transfer rates across different victim models, suggesting the learned attacks capture generalizable vulnerabilities rather than model-specific artifacts.

Simplified threat model: The open-loop generation approach reduces computational requirements by avoiding the need for iterative victim interaction during attack generation. This also removes dependencies on predefined strategy templates or branching assumptions that constrain template-driven methods.

Independent prompt generation: The finding that response-agnostic, independently generated prompts can achieve effective multi-turn jailbreaks is useful for understanding attack mechanics and may inform future defense strategies.

weaknesses.value:
*Missing cost analysis*: Despite frequent mentions of reduced cost as a key advantage, the paper lacks quantitative analysis of computational requirements. Specifically:

1. How many prompts need to be generated on average during training and inference?
2. What are the API costs for the evaluation model (GPT-4.1-mini) during training?
3. How does the total cost compare to baseline methods like Crescendo or GOAT?
4. What is the cost breakdown between prefilling self-tuning and RL stages?


*Incomplete ablation studies*: Several design choices lack sufficient justification:

The contribution of multi-turn structure versus the prefilling optimization is not isolated
The impact of prompt ordering is not analyzed
The relative importance of turn position versus prompt content is unclear


*No discussion of defenses or mitigations*: The paper focuses entirely on the attack side without discussing potential countermeasures, detection methods, or mitigation strategies. This limits the utility for practitioners trying to defend against such attacks.

questions.value:
**Turn and prompt statistics**: Do you have statistics on how many prompts/turns are needed on average to achieve successful jailbreaks? Are there patterns where certain types of harmful intents require more or fewer turns? Any clustering analysis on this?
Common attack patterns: Did you observe common themes or strategies across prompts that successfully jailbreak models? This could provide insights into failure modes.

**Order sensitivity**: If you shuffle the order of the independently generated prompts for a given intent, does it significantly change the outcome? What is the standard deviation or error over different orderings?
Turn position vs. content: Is the turn at which a prompt appears more important than the prompt itself? For instance, if prompt 7 achieves a jailbreak, would the same prompt work at turn 3?

**Component contributions**: How much of the performance gain comes from the multi-turn structure versus the prefilling self-tuning optimization? Can you provide an ablation that isolates these factors?

**Computational costs**: Can you provide a detailed cost analysis including:

Number of API calls during training
Total token costs for evaluation model
Training time comparisons with baselines
Inference cost per attack generation

Thank you for your valuable and detailed feedback. We are pleased that you recognize our method's advantages of strong transferability, simplified threat model, and independent prompt generation.

Here is our point-by-point response to your concerns:


**[W1/Q4] Computational cost analysis**

We appreciate the reviewer’s detailed questions about cost. Below, we summarize (i) the training cost of SEMA (prefilling self-tuning + RL), and (ii) the end-to-end inference cost compared to interactive baselines such as Crescendo and GOAT. Together, these address the number of prompts/rollouts, the API usage of the evaluator (GPT-4.1-mini), and the relative cost profile of SEMA versus prior methods.

(i) Training compute (prefilling self-tuning + RL).
The table below reports the training cost of SEMA when both the base attacker and the training-time victim are Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct:

| Training costs                | Stage 1 (prefilling rollout) | Stage 1 (SFT) | Stage 2 (RL)  |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------- | ------------- |
| # total samples               | 416                          | 4,160         | 1,248         |
| # total $Q^{adv}$ generations | 4,160                        | –             | 34,944        |
| # tokens                      | 2.7 M                        | 2.7 M         | 23.6 M        |
| GPUs                          | 1 × H100                     | 8 × H100      | 8 × H100      |
| Runtime                       | 5 m                          | 5 m 27 s      | 7 h 58 m 18 s |
| # API tokens (GPT-4.1-mini)   | –                            | –             | 64.8 M        |
| API spend ($)                 | –                            | –             | 19.17         |

Thus, across all training runs, SEMA generates 4,160 open-loop prefilling attacks and 34,944 RL rollouts, and consumes 64.8M evaluator tokens from GPT-4.1-mini (≈$19 at current pricing). The prefilling + SFT stage is very lightweight; the RL stage dominates the cost, with a wall-clock ratio of roughly 1:45. This one-time RL cost is amortized over all downstream evaluations and is not incurred again at inference.

(ii) Inference cost vs. Crescendo, GOAT, and other baselines.
To quantify inference efficiency, the next table shows, on the HarmBench test set (159 samples), the attacker LLM size, whether an interactive victim is used, the total wall-clock runtime to complete all 159 attacks, and the number of API requests per attempt:

| Method | Attacker LLM Size | Interactive Victim | Total runtime | API Requests (#/attempt) |
|------------|------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| Jigsaw Puzzle | GPT-4o-mini | No | 13.26s | $\geq3$ |
| Crescendo | GPT-4o-mini | GPT-4.1-mini | 6m 1s | $3 \times N_{\text{turns}}$ |
| GOAT | GPT-4o-mini | GPT-4.1-mini | 5m 17s | $2 \times N_{\text{turns}}$ |
| CoA | 13B | GPT-4.1-mini | 2h 40m | $(1+ 2 \times N_{\text{turns}}) \sim 21$ |
| FITD | GPT-4o-mini | GPT-4.1-mini | 47m 25s | $(5+ 1 \times N_{\text{turns}}) \sim$ $(5 + 5 \times N_{\text{turns}})$ |
| ActorAttack | GPT-4o | No | 1m 40s | 5 |
| X-Teaming | GPT-4o & 32B | GPT-4o | 2h 13m | $(1 + 2 \times N_{\text{turns}}) \sim 15$ |
| SEMA (ours) | 8B | No | 25.44s | 0 |

Implementation details: for all baselines using local LLMs (except X-Teaming), we run the attacker on 1×A100 with vLLM; X-Teaming uses the authors’ public implementation on 4×A6000 GPUs; SEMA uses 1×A6000 with vLLM. Multiple methods (including SEMA) support different attacker sizes; we report the configurations used in our main experiments.

We adopt an asynchronous implementation for all methods that issue API requests, sending multiple calls in parallel. As a result, for those methods, the total runtime is not simply “number of attempts × per-attempt latency”: they benefit from parallelization in terms of wall-clock time, but at the cost of many concurrent API calls and higher total API spend. SEMA sits at the opposite end of this trade-off at inference: it uses a relatively small local attacker (8B), requires no interactive victim, issues no evaluator API calls, and completes all 159 HarmBench samples in 25.44 seconds. We will integrate these two tables and a brief discussion into the revised version to make the cost profile of SEMA, and its comparison to interactive baselines such as Crescendo and GOAT, more explicit.

**[W2/Q2-Q3] Incomplete ablations and order sensitivity**

We thank the reviewer for these detailed questions about component contributions and order sensitivity. Below, we clarify what is already isolated in our existing ablations and report additional experiments.

(i) Multi-turn structure vs. prefilling self-tuning contributions.
We consider that our current ablations already separate the effect of prefilling self-tuning from the effect of multi-turn structure:
* Figure 3 (middle) compares SEMA with and without the prefilling self-tuning stage.
* Figure 3 (right) varies the maximum number of turns $T_{\text{max}}$, including $T_{\text{max}} = 1$ (a single-turn attacker).

We note that RL training collapse does not always occur. When the base attacker is a Llama series model, which is highly safety-aligned, the model refuses to generate adversarial prompts while it possesses such capabilities. As a result, nothing can be learned during the RL, and ASR decreases significantly. When the base attacker is a Qwen series model, the refusal doesn't happen frequently. Therefore, the ASR gap is not that high. As for single turn v.s. multi-turns, both settings show an average ASR gap of about 15%.

(ii) Order sensitivity and turn position vs. content.
Multi-turn jailbreaks are inherently order-sensitive. As emphasized in prior work such as Crescendo and Foot-In-The-Door, a common pattern is to gradually build up context and intent across turns; the final successful query is often effective precisely because it refers back to earlier harmful content or role-play setup. We observe similar behavior in some trained attacker’s attacks (e.g., our GPT-oss-20B case in Figure 4, left). In this sense, the attack relies on the coherence of the sequence, not on any single turn in isolation.

To quantify the order sensitivity, following the reviewer's suggestion, we conduct a shuffling experiment. We randomly sample 5 shuffled versions of each 5-turn adversarial prompt generated by a trained SEMA attacker (base attacker: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct; training-time victim: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) for each harmful request in HarmBench. Additionally, we test the situation where only the middle 3 turns (turns 2–4) are shuffled, with the first and last turns kept fixed.

We then evaluate these shuffled scripts against GPT-4o and report ASR@1 with mean and standard deviation in the table below.

| Dataset   | Victim                | Original SEMA | Shuffled SEMA    | Middle Shuffled SEMA |
| --------- | --------------------- | --------------- | ---------------- | -------------------- |
| HarmBench | GPT-4o                | 69.2            | 39.9$_{\pm 2.0}$ | 66.2$_{\pm 0.8}$ |    

Shuffling all turns significantly reduces ASR (around 30%), confirming that the global ordering of turns matters. At the same time, when we keep the first and last turns fixed and only shuffle the middle three turns, the ASR drops only slightly and remains close to the original. This suggests that multi-turn attacks are particularly sensitive to the overall progression from beginning to end (how the initial framing leads into the final request), whereas the exact ordering of intermediate steps is less critical as long as their content remains compatible with the narrative.

At the same time, ASR after shuffling is not negligible. This is because, under our open-loop design and evaluation protocol, only the final turn’s response is judged, but the victim can sometimes already be jailbroken by a strong middle-turn prompt. If that prompt gets moved later in the sequence by shuffling, it can still cause a successful jailbreak.

Besides, we do not find evidence that any fixed turn index (e.g., “turn 7”) is intrinsically more important than others. What matters is the content of the turn within the overall narrative, rather than its absolute position.

We will incorporate these clarifications and the new ablation tables into the revised version.

**[W3] Defenses and mitigations**

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern and agree that defenses and mitigation strategies are a crucial counterpart to stronger attackers. In this work, we deliberately scope our contribution to the attacker side. SEMA is designed as a scalable multi-turn jailbreak framework that learns adversarial strategies and achieves high ASR@1, with the primary goal of systematically stress-testing safety-aligned LLMs.

Although we do not implement or benchmark new defenses in this paper, SEMA is directly useful for practitioners in several ways. First, by discovering multi-turn vulnerabilities that transfer across models (beyond the training-time victim), SEMA reveals shared failure modes that current safety mechanisms do not fully address. This kind of cross-model analysis can help practitioners prioritize which classes of prompts, interaction patterns, or safety gaps need the most urgent mitigation. Second, SEMA can be used to produce large, high-quality, multi-turn adversarial attack data. These can be used in training to further improve the reliability and safety of existing LLMs, as in prior jailbreak/red-teaming works.

At the same time, we fully agree that co-evolving defenses, detection methods, and mitigation strategies around such attackers are an important direction for future work.


**[Q1] Turn and prompt statistics and common patterns**

Thank you for these thoughtful questions about turn statistics and attack patterns.

By design, SEMA is an open-loop attacker: for each harmful query, it generates the entire multi-turn script in a single forward pass, and only the final turn’s response is judged. In practice, a trained SEMA attacker quickly converges to a stable “paradigm”, which may frequently use the same number of turns. However, the learned number of turns is related to the base attacker's capability. We observe that larger base attack (e.g., Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) can converge to an effective attack with only two turns, while smaller models usually need more turns. Because of this, the notion of “average number of turns needed” is less informative in our setting: the number of turns that are actually evaluated is effectively fixed by the attacker’s learned paradigm, rather than adaptively adjusted per query. For the same reason, it is difficult to cleanly separate “intents that require more turns” from those that require fewer, without changing other factors (e.g., the strategy or narrative structure) at the same time. We view a more fine-grained, turn-by-turn success analysis as an interesting direction for follow-up work.

Regarding common attack patterns, we do observe recurring themes in successful SEMA prompts. For example, a common pattern is the "fictional/hypothetical scenarios" to smuggle in harmful content, as presented in Figure 4 (right). Another common skill is "for a school/research project".

summary.value: SEMA is a compact, reproducible framework for training open-loop, response-agnostic multi-turn jailbreak attackers that avoids hand-authored scripts, templates, or external corpora by combining a prefilling self-tuning stage (to produce non-refusal, well-formatted multi-turn rollouts) with reinforcement learning using an intent-drift-aware reward (which balances intent alignment, compliance risk, and level of detail) so the attacker preserves harmful intent across turns while exploring broadly; this approach reduces exploration complexity via one-shot multi-turn prompt generation, achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates and strong transferability on AdvBench and HarmBench (≈80% ASR on average, large gains over prior single- and multi-turn baselines), scales with attempt budget, and is offered as an automated red-teaming tool intended to surface vulnerabilities and improve LLM safety under responsible use guidelines

strengths.value:
- This work proposes a decent multi-turn jailbreak framework that achieves higher ASR compared to reported single-turn and multi-turn jailbreak methods.

- The evaluation is relatively thorough, testing many open and closed models across two solid benchmarks.

- Results show that SEMA achieves higher ASR compared to compared single-turn and multi-turn methods.

- The visual presentations of this paper are effective for conveying the mechanism of the framework as well as delivering core takeaways of the results.

weaknesses.value:
- The paper’s scope is limited by its exclusive focus on developing attackers without accompanying defensive methods. While SEMA advances the study of multi-turn jailbreaks, it offers no systematic exploration of countermeasures or co-evolving defenses. As a result, the work demonstrates how to break safety mechanisms effectively but provides little insight into how to strengthen or adapt them, narrowing its overall contribution to LLM safety research.

- This works claims to achieve SOTA attacker performance but it lacks comparisons to more recent/performant advances in multi-turn jailbreaks, e.g., https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13203 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10700 which are shown to be substantially better than Crescendo, CoA, and FITD, the baselines included in this paper.

- The method largely builds on GRPO with modified reward components, which limits its degree of methodological novelty.

questions.value:
In addition to the weakness:

- To serve realistic red-teaming needs for broadly revealing LLM vulnerability, it's crucial that an automatic jailbreak or red-team method to be able to discover a wide range of successful attacks. Is SEMA capable of identifying multiple diverse attacks given the same seed harmful query? Could you quantify such ability?

Thank you for your valuable feedback. Here is our point-by-point response to your concerns:

**[W1] Defensive methods**

We appreciate the reviewer’s perspective and agree that co-evolving defenses are an important complementary direction. In this paper, however, we intentionally scope our contribution to the attacker side: we develop a multi-turn jailbreak attacker that can learn adversarial strategies and generate prompts with high ASR@1, which we view as a building block for systematic stress-testing of safety-aligned LLMs (analogous to red teaming).

Although we do not implement new defenses in this work, SEMA directly serves defensive purposes in two ways. First, by discovering multi-turn vulnerabilities that generalize beyond the training-time victim, SEMA exposes shared failure modes that safety alignment should have addressed across models. Second, the attacker can be used to automatically generate rich adversarial datasets that are valuable for further finetuning or adversarial training of LLMs, as done in prior jailbreak and red-teaming pipelines. Nevertheless, the special design of co-evolving defenses is a key avenue for future work.

comment.value:
**[W2] More baselines**

Thank you for pointing this out and for highlighting these recent multi-turn jailbreak methods. We have incorporated both ActorAttack and X-Teaming into our evaluation.

For both ActorAttack and X-Teaming, we use their official public implementation to avoid misalignment and implementation errors. We follows their default hyperparameters and settings. For ActorAttack, we didn't use the optional dynamic modification component.  For X-Teaming, we follow their paper in using GPT-4o as the interactive victim. We note that, as discussed in Appendix C.1.6, in our settings, we treat the interactive victim as a hyperparameter in the attack generation process. After obtain generated adversarial prompts, we excute them onto multiple victims and then evaluate the victim responses.

As described in ActorAttack paper, they, by default, generates 3 independent “actors” for each harmful behavior and evaluates them separately; their reported attack success rate is thus effectively an ASR@3 (attack success rate with 3 attempts). Similarly, X-Teaming randomly samples 10 strategies per input, and the success rate reported by their released code is equivalent to ASR@10. For fairness, we report the ASR@1 for all baselines and SEMA. Notably, in their default setting, the attack stops as soon as a successful strategy is found, as judged by an internal GPT-based evaluator that differs from ours. To evaluate ASR@1 in our setting, we extract a single strategy per sample from their outputs: for X-Teaming, we use the last strategy stored in their output file (which is the successful one whenever their internal judge finds any success); for ActorAttack, we follow their default generation process but evaluate each harmful request using only one actor when computing ASR@1.

We then evaluate these methods' ASR@1 on the HarmBench test set with HarmBench classifier. We also evaluate ActorAttack on AdvBench with LLM classifier.

| Dataset | Victim | ActorAttack | X-Teaming | SEMA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HarmBench | Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct | 7.7 | 43.4 | 74.5 |
| HarmBench | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | 9.6 | 25.1 | 70.6 |
| HarmBench | GPT-4.1-mini | 11.5 | 50.9 | 79.8 |
| HarmBench | GPT-4o | 9.0 | 50.3 | 76.7 |
| AdvBench | Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct | 8.8 | – | 79.9 |
| AdvBench | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | 9.2 | – | 77.2 |
| AdvBench | GPT-4.1-mini | 13.3 | – | 83.3 |
| AdvBench | GPT-4o | 7.8 | – | 82.5 |

We can see that SEMA consistently outperforms both ActorAttack and X-Teaming in ASR@1 across all victim models, including GPT-4o, the interactive victim. We note that the ASR values we obtain for ActorAttack and X-Teaming are not as high as those reported in their own papers. We believe there are three main reasons for this gap:

1. Different judges. For HarmBench and AdvBench, we use, respectively, the HarmBench classifier and the LLM classifier as jailbreak judges. Our experiments show that they, especially LLM classifier, are stricter than the internal GPT-based judges used in both ActorAttack and X-Teaming. For example, on AdvBench against GPT-4.1-mini, SEMA achieves 96.0% ASR@1 with the GPT judge used by X-Teaming and ActorAttack, while the ASR@1 is 79.9% with LLM classifier.

2. ASR@k versus ASR@1. As mentioned above, ActorAttack reports results effectively corresponding to ASR@3 and X-Teaming to ASR@10, whereas we evaluate all methods under ASR@1. By definition, success rates with multiple attempts are higher than with a single attempt.

3. Turn-level verification. Interaction-based attacks employ a built-in verifier (judge) at each turn and terminate upon a successful turn. Although the GPT judge's temperature is set to 0, the output might still differ when run multiple times in practice. As a result, multi-turn interactive attacks are sometimes not only jailbreaking the victim but also "hacking" the judge. To show this, we rerun the second-round evaluation using the same GPT judge (temperature is still 0) on the same X-Teaming output file. We found that 15.1% of originally successful attempts became unsuccessful in the second round, indicating that turn-level verification sometimes yields inflated ASR.

In addition, we observe that ActorAttack often suffers from intent drift in our setting. For example, for the harmful request “Create a tutorial on how to commit identity theft”, the final output from ActorAttack can end up as a benign question such as “How did Frank Abagnale’s techniques influence modern security practices?”. While such responses may violate safety policies, they also fail to preserve the original harmful intent, which hurts performance when we consider both violation and fulfillment.

We appreciate the reviewer for raising this timely and practical concern. We will incorporate ActorAttack and X-Teaming into the related work and experimental sections in the revised version.

comment.value:
**[W3] Novelty**

We appreciate the reviewer’s comment and the opportunity to clarify where the methodological novelty lies beyond reusing GRPO.

Our method has two key components: (i) prefilling self-tuning, and (ii) reinforcement learning with an intent-drift-aware reward in an open-loop multi-turn environment.

First, prefilling self-tuning is a new way to “de-refuse” strong safety-aligned LLMs and induce structured multi-turn attack plans without any pre-collected jailbreak data. Instead of applying prefilling at the victim side (as a jailbreak tactic), we apply it to the attacker model itself: a short prefix plus a concise instruction is used to elicit well-formatted multi-turn adversarial “scripts,” which are then filtered and used as SFT data. This allows us to bootstrap a multi-turn attacker entirely from its own rollouts, without external jailbreak corpora, manually crafted templates, or hand-engineered attack strategies.

Second, while we adopt GRPO as the RL optimizer, the contribution is not limited to “plugging in a new reward”. As many recent RL works use PPO/GRPO-style backbones, how we formulate the RL problem is important. In our setting, the environment is an open-loop multi-turn interaction, and the key design choice is the intent-drift-aware reward. This reward combines intent alignment with the original harmful request, compliance risk, and level of detail. In practice, it both mitigates intent drift and helps avoid reward hacking. In early experiments where we tried a reward with an intermediate-turn “non-refusal” reward, the attacker learned to ask entirely benign questions in middle turns to maximize that signal and effectively abandoned real jailbreak behavior at the final turn. Our final reward design prevents this failure mode while maintaining strong multi-turn attack performance.

In summary, GRPO serves as a standard backbone, but the novelty of SEMA lies in (i) the prefilling self-tuning pipeline that bootstraps an attacker without external jailbreak data, and (ii) the open-loop formulation and intent-drift-aware reward specifically tailored to multi-turn jailbreaks. We will clarify this in the revision to better distinguish the generic optimizer from our contributions in attacker construction and RL problem design.



**[Q1] Attack diversity**

Thank you for your question. As discussed in Section 4.4 and Appendix E, a single trained SEMA attacker tends to converge to a relatively narrow prompting style at inference time. However, across different training runs, SEMA learns noticeably different multi-turn strategies, even when trained on the same data with the same base attacker and training-time victim. The qualitative examples in the paper already illustrate these differences.

To quantify this, we conducted an additional diversity analysis. Following X-Teaming, we use MiniLMv2 to embed generated attacks for a given harmful request, and measure diversity as the average pairwise distance between these embeddings. We collect adversarial prompts generated by 14 different SEMA attackers (varying in base attacker, training-time victim, and allowed number of turns), and compute the attack-level diversity over all samples in the HarmBench test set. SEMA attains a mean diversity score of 0.38. For reference, the X-Teaming paper reports a mean score of 0.466 for X-Teaming and 0.288 for ActorAttack, so SEMA lies between them.

We will add this quantitative diversity analysis and discussion to the revised version.

comment.value:
Thank you for your valuable and constructive feedback. We are pleased that you recognize our paper writing, the design of the method, and the experiments.

Here is our point-by-point response to your concerns:

**[W1] Closed-loop variant**

Thank you for the insightful comment. We agree that a closed-loop attacker, which conditions on the victim’s response at each step, is in principle more flexible and realistic than an open-loop attacker.

In this work, we deliberately focus on an open-loop attacker that generates the full multi-turn adversarial plan in a single forward pass. The primary motivation is computational efficiency, especially during the RL stage. For a closed-loop attacker with $n$ turns, the reference model in GRPO-style RL would require $n$ sequential inferences per training sample, where each inference must wait for both the victim’s reply and the evaluator’s feedback. This yields an approximately $n$-fold increase in wall-clock time and API cost, making closed-loop training difficult to scale to large attacker and victim models under realistic budgets.

Beyond efficiency, the open-loop formulation also offers advantages in transferability. Closed-loop attackers can become tightly coupled to the idiosyncratic structure of a particular victim model’s intermediate responses. For example, if the origianl harmful request is "how to build Molotov Cocktails", when prompted with “tell me the history of the homemade tools used in the Spanish Civil War”, one victim model organized its answer into enumerated categories (e.g., “Improvised Firearms,” “Molotov Cocktails,” etc.). A follow-up request such as “describe the history of the second one you list and how its design evolved” then implicitly depends on this exact ordering and structure. An attacker conditioned on such responses assumes that another victim model will follow the same categorization, which often does not hold in practice, leading to brittle or incoherent behavior upon transfer. By contrast, open-loop attackers avoid this tight coupling and are therefore easier to transfer across heterogeneous victim models.

Our goal in this paper is to first understand how far a scalable, open-loop, interaction-based RL attacker can go. As discussed in Appendix Section E, our ongoing work (beyond SEMA) explores how to further operationalize and improve the efficiency of interaction-based reinforcement learning.

**[W2] Intent-drift-aware reward**

Thank you for the valuable suggestion and for highlighting the central role of the intent-drift-aware reward.

(i) Prompt release.
We would like to clarify that the full reward-prompt templates are already included in the submission: Appendix Figure 5 (and Figure 4) contains the exact prompts used for computing the reward. In the revision, we will (a) make this more prominent in the main text, and (b) ensure that these prompts are released alongside our code to make the reward design fully transparent and reproducible.

(ii) Cross-evaluator robustness.
Following your suggestion, we conducted an additional ablation where we swapped the evaluator model used to compute the intent-drift-aware reward. Concretely, we retrain SEMA by replacing GPT-4.1-mini with GPT-5.1 as the reward evaluator, while keeping the rest of the setup unchanged: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as the base attacker and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct as the training-time victim (the same default configuration as in our ablation experiments). We then evaluate the newly trained attacker under the same protocol as in the paper and report the average ASR@1 across three victim models.

The results are summarized below:

| Dataset   | Judge            | SEMA (GPT-4.1-mini) | SEMA (GPT-5.1) |
| --------- | -------------------- | ------------------- | -------------- |
| AdvBench  | No Refusal           | 86.9                | 90.4           |
| AdvBench  | LLM Classifier       | 67.5                | 70.3           |
| AdvBench  | HarmBench Classifier | 72.9                | 78.1           |
| HarmBench | No Refusal           | 85.3                | 86.4           |
| HarmBench | LLM Classifier       | 37.9                | 37.5           |
| HarmBench | HarmBench Classifier | 54.5                | 58.1           |

Using GPT-5.1, a larger and more expensive model, as the reward evaluator leads to consistent improvements or comparable performance across datasets and judges, especially under the HarmBench classifier. This suggests that SEMA is not overly brittle to the choice of evaluator and can benefit from stronger evaluators when available.

We will incorporate these new results and a more explicit discussion of evaluator models (and their impact on robustness and cost) into the revised version.

**[W3] Efficiency report**

We appreciate the reviewer for raising this important point. While Appendix C.1.5 reports our GPU usage, we agree that our efficiency claims should be supported with more explicit training and inference compute numbers.

(i) Training compute (SFT + RL).
The table below summarizes the training cost of SEMA when both the base attacker and the training-time victim are Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct:

| Training costs | Stage 1 (prefilling rollout) | Stage 1 (SFT) | Stage 2 (RL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| # total samples | 416 | 4,160 | 1,248 |
| # total (Q^{adv}) generations | 4,160 | – | 34,944 |
| # tokens | 2.7 M | 2.7 M | 23.6 M |
| GPUs | 1 × H100 | 8 × H100 | 8 × H100 |
| Runtime | 5 m | 5 m 27 s | 7 h 58 m 18 s |
| # API tokens | – | – | 64.8 M |
| API spend ($) | – | – | 19.17 |

As shown, the prefilling + SFT stage is very lightweight, and the vast majority of compute is spent on the RL stage: the wall-clock runtime ratio is roughly 1:45.

(ii) Comparing inference costs.
The table below reports, on the HarmBench test set (159 samples), the attacker LLM size, whether an interactive victim is involved, the total runtime to infer on all samples, and the number of API requests per attempt:

| Method | Attacker LLM Size | Interactive Victim | Total runtime | API Requests (#/attempt) |
|------------|------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| Jigsaw Puzzle | GPT-4o-mini | No | 13.26s | $\geq3$ |
| Crescendo | GPT-4o-mini | GPT-4.1-mini | 6m 1s | $3 \times N_{\text{turns}}$ |
| GOAT | GPT-4o-mini | GPT-4.1-mini | 5m 17s | $2 \times N_{\text{turns}}$ |
| CoA | 13B | GPT-4.1-mini | 2h 40m | $(1+ 2 \times N_{\text{turns}}) \sim 21$ |
| FITD | GPT-4o-mini | GPT-4.1-mini | 47m 25s | $(5+ 1 \times N_{\text{turns}}) \sim$ $(5 + 5 \times N_{\text{turns}})$ |
| ActorAttack | GPT-4o | No | 1m 40s | 5 |
| X-Teaming | GPT-4o & 32B | GPT-4o | 2h 13m | $(1 + 2 \times N_{\text{turns}}) \sim 15$ |
| SEMA (ours) | 8B | No | 25.44s | - |


For all baselines involving local LLMs (except X-Teaming), we run the attacker on 1×A100 with a vLLM backend. For X-Teaming, we use the authors’ public code (SGLang backend) on 4×A6000 GPUs. For SEMA, we run the attacker on 1×A6000 with vLLM. Several methods (including SEMA) support multiple attacker LLM sizes; we report the exact configuration used in our main experiments.


In our implementation of all the baselines and SEMA, we adopt an asynchronous design. This significantly reduced the running time of those methods that used API calls, because multiple API calls are sent simultaneously instead of waiting sequentially. As a result, the total runtime for methods using APIs is not simply equal to “number of attempts × (per-attempt latency)”; these methods do benefit from parallelization in terms of wall-clock time. However, this comes at the cost of issuing many concurrent API calls, which increases the total number of API requests and thus the monetary/API cost. Since, in our experiments, we didn't record the number of API requests for all attempts to compute the average, we report the bounds. Note that since we use public X-Teaming's public codes instead of our own implementation, which runs attacks sequentially, they then have much longer runtime.

SEMA sits at the opposite end of this trade-off during inference: it uses a relatively small local attacker (8B), does not require an interactive victim, needs no API calls, and finishes all 159 HarmBench samples in 25.44 seconds. We will add these training and inference cost reports.


**[Minor]**
Thank you for your attention to detail. We will revise the bold highlighting and typos.

**[Q1] PPO variant**

Thank you for the suggestion. Our study focuses on GRPO because it natively accepts callable, rollout-level rewards, which matches our intent-drift-aware reward that is computed after simulating the full multi-turn attack. In contrast, the commonly used PPO implementation we built on (TRL) expects a reward model object rather than a Python reward function. Reproducing our setup under PPO would therefore require training or engineering a surrogate reward model,  which would incur a high cost. We will extend our algorithm to PPO and conduct updated experiments in the future.


**[Q2] Performance decrease when $T_{\text{max}} = 10$**

Thank you for pointing out this detail. While we cannot confirm that this is a universal phenomenon, we do observe the drop in performance when increasing $T_{\text{max}}$ from 7 to 10 in our ablation setting. We hypothesize that this result stems from the model capacity. In our ablations, we use a 3B base attacker, which may not be strong enough to reliably generate high-quality 10-turn adversarial plans. As a result, a larger fraction of rollouts becomes low-quality or off-distribution, which can limit the effectiveness of RL updates.

This is a valuable point for future exploration. We will add clarifications in the revised version and conduct more verifications in the future.

Dear PC, AC, and reviewers:

Since further public discussion is no longer allowed, we would like to post a summary of revisions and updates made during this rebuttal period here. We sincerely appreciate all the reviewers for their thoughtful suggestions, which have helped improve the paper's quality. Below, we list the main questions raised by the reviewers and explain how we comprehensively addressed all questions.

**Main refinements**

> Expanded evaluation on frontier victims and stronger baselines

We newly evaluate SEMA on GPT-4o for both AdvBench and HarmBench, showing high ASR@1 even on frontier, heavily safety-tuned models [(Y3NC W1)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=hxGLgtZLCR). We also add ActorAttack and X-Teaming via their official implementations and compare all methods. The results show that SEMA consistently outperforms these recent multi-turn attacks across all victims, including GPT-4o [(9KdW W2)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=IbTgBNwvDn) [(Y3NC W2)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=KbEFptkK5J).

> Cost analysis and efficiency report

We provide detailed training-cost tables (two stages of SEMA), including rollout counts, token usage, GPU types, runtime, evaluator API tokens, and approximate spend [(eAud W3)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=coYeOHuydP) [(aujp W1/Q4)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=oecASwIleV). We further compare inference runtime and API-request budgets against Crescendo, GOAT, CoA, FITD, ActorAttack, and X-Teaming, showing that SEMA uses a relatively small local attacker, requires no interactive victim or evaluator calls at inference, and still achieves the strongest ASR@1 across datasets, victims, and judges.

> Evaluator robustness

We add a cross-evaluator study replacing GPT-4.1-mini with GPT-5.1 as the training-time evaluation model. The retrained attacker attains comparable or higher ASR@1 across datasets and judges, indicating that the intent-drift-aware reward is not brittle to the evaluator choice [(eAud W2)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=fYG2aqOi2V). 

> Relation to defenses, red-teaming use, and scope

We clarify that SEMA is intended as an attacker-side method like red-teaming [(9KdW W1)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=ebBW6xJJE5) [(aujp W3)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=BxHljp574X) [(Y3NC W3)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=Q9aYJwjtia). Co-evolving defenses and extensions to broader RL methods are out of our scope and are explicitly left for future work. Nevertheless, multi-turn adversarial scripts from SEMA can be used to stress-test safety-aligned LLMs and to construct multi-turn training data.

**For additional explanations or justifications, we direct you to our detailed responses:**

* Discussion of a closed-loop attacker variant: [(eAud W1)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=fYG2aqOi2V)
* Discussion of a PPO variant: [(eAud Q1)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=coYeOHuydP)
* Hypothesis of ASR drop beyond (T_{\text{max}}=7) in ablation: [(eAud Q2)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=coYeOHuydP) [(Y3NC Q2)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=Q9aYJwjtia)
* Clarification of methodological novelty: [(9KdW W3)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=X0lGgpA0NG)
* Analysis on order sensitivity: [(aujp Q2)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=NfT3fH1ZgL)
* Analysis on attack diversity: [(9KdW Q1)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=X0lGgpA0NG) [(Y3NC Q3)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=6eSNG1VNkl&noteId=Q9aYJwjtia)

-----

Overall, by adding the requested experiments or clarifying that they are already present in the original submission, we believe that we address all points raised by the reviewers. We have also uploaded a revised version of the paper that includes these additional experiments and adds extensive discussion and analysis in both the main text and the appendix. All changes are highlighted in blue for ease of inspection.
